```{python}
#| include: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from IPython.display import Markdown

plt.rcParams.update({"axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
```

## Question

"Is AI a bubble?" cannot be answered directly: nobody can measure a bubble, and whether it
bursts is a prediction, not a fact in any dataset. So the first job is to turn the vague
question into questions data **can** answer. A bubble is usually described by three signs:

| A bubble means … | We measure | Source |
|:--|:--|:--|
| prices far above what the companies earn | the cyclically adjusted price/earnings ratio (CAPE) of US stocks | Shiller |
| prices that rose unusually fast | the NASDAQ index compared with five years earlier | FRED |
| everybody talking about it | the share of Hacker News story titles that mention AI | HN Search API |

Our question: **how do today's values of these three signs compare with earlier booms**, the
1929 crash, the dot-com bubble of 2000 and the crypto boom of 2017–2021?

## Data

All three were downloaded with `fetch.py` and saved unchanged in `data/`.

```{python}
shiller = pd.read_excel("data/shiller-ie_data.xls", sheet_name="Data", header=None, skiprows=8)
nasdaq = pd.read_csv("data/fred-nasdaqcom.csv")
hn = pd.read_csv("data/hn-title-mentions.csv")
print(shiller.shape, nasdaq.shape, hn.shape)
```

- **Shiller** (shillerdata.com): monthly S&P composite prices, earnings and CAPE from 1871.
  CAPE divides the price by the average inflation-adjusted earnings of the past ten years.
- **NASDAQ Composite** (FRED series NASDAQCOM): the daily close since 1971, dominated by
  technology companies.
- **Hacker News**: for every month since March 2007, the number of story titles and the number
  that contain each term as a whole word, from the HN Search API by Algolia.

What it cannot tell us: all three describe the *US* market and an English-speaking tech forum.
Hacker News readers are not the public. And none of it says what the future holds.

## Cleaning

Shiller's sheet has eight lines of headings and notes at the bottom. Its dates are numbers like
`2026.1`, which means October (`.10`), not January (`.01`): read as a decimal year it would
put October before February. We rebuild the month from the text.

```{python}
shiller = shiller[pd.to_numeric(shiller[0], errors="coerce").notna()]
year_month = shiller[0].map(lambda x: f"{x:.2f}")   # 2026.1 -> "2026.10"
cape = pd.Series(pd.to_numeric(shiller[12], errors="coerce").to_numpy(),
                 index=pd.to_datetime(year_month, format="%Y.%m"), name="CAPE").dropna()
print(f"CAPE {cape.index.min():%Y-%m} to {cape.index.max():%Y-%m}")
```

FRED marks days without a value (holidays) with an empty field. We keep the month-end close,
for complete months only: the data was downloaded in early November 2026, so we stop at October,
the last month all three sources cover.

```{python}
nasdaq["date"] = pd.to_datetime(nasdaq["observation_date"])
close = pd.to_numeric(nasdaq["NASDAQCOM"], errors="coerce")
nasdaq = pd.Series(close.to_numpy(), index=nasdaq["date"]).dropna()
nasdaq = nasdaq.loc[:"2026-10-31"].resample("ME").last()
growth5 = nasdaq / nasdaq.shift(60)   # value now / value five years (60 months) earlier
```

Hacker News grew a lot, so raw counts mostly measure the site's growth. We use the **share**
of all story titles. A title can contain several terms, so we do not add them up.

```{python}
hn["month"] = pd.to_datetime(hn["month"])
hn = hn.set_index("month")
shares = hn[["AI", "LLM", "GPT", "blockchain", "bitcoin", "crypto"]].div(hn["all_stories"], axis=0)
```

## Exploration

```{python}
#| label: fig-cape
#| fig-cap: "CAPE of the S&P composite, 1881 to today."
ax = cape.plot(figsize=(8, 3.5), color="black", lw=1)
for when, label in [("1929-09", "1929"), ("1999-12", "2000"), (cape.index.max(), "today")]:
    v = cape.loc[when] if not isinstance(when, str) else cape.loc[when].iloc[0]
    ax.annotate(f"{label}: {v:.0f}", (pd.Timestamp(when), v), xytext=(0, 6),
                textcoords="offset points", ha="center")
ax.set_ylabel("CAPE")
ax.set_xlabel("")
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-hn
#| fig-cap: "Share of Hacker News story titles that mention each term."
ax = (shares[["AI", "bitcoin", "crypto"]].rolling(3).mean() * 100).plot(figsize=(8, 3.5), lw=2)
ax.set_ylabel("% of story titles")
ax.set_xlabel("")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()
```

## Analysis

Where does today's value of each sign rank in its own history?

```{python}
def rank(series, label, unit=""):
    now = series.dropna().iloc[-1]
    return {"sign": label, "today": f"{now:.1f}{unit}",
            "higher than … of all months": f"{(series.dropna() < now).mean():.0%}",
            "record": f"{series.max():.1f}{unit} ({series.idxmax():%b %Y})"}

table = pd.DataFrame([
    rank(cape, "CAPE"),
    rank(growth5, "NASDAQ vs 5 years earlier", "×"),
    rank(shares["AI"] * 100, "HN titles mentioning AI", " %"),
])
Markdown(table.to_markdown(index=False))
```

## Conclusions & limitations

On two of the three signs, AI today looks like a boom. US stocks are priced higher relative to
earnings than at any time except the months around 2000, and higher than before the 1929 crash.
Talk about AI on Hacker News is close to its peak of February 2026, about four times the highest
share bitcoin ever had. The third sign is **not** there: the NASDAQ is 1.6 times its value five
years ago, an ordinary pace (higher than only 40% of months), far from 5.9 times in 2000.

What the data **cannot** say is whether this is a bubble. High valuations can last for years, and
if AI raises earnings as much as the market expects, today's prices may turn out reasonable. The
honest answer: *two of the three signs that preceded earlier crashes are present; whether a
crash follows is not in the data.*

Limitations:

- Three signs are our choice. Others (debt, new investors, company spending) could disagree.
- Every source is about the US or an English-language tech forum.
- A word count is a crude measure of attention, and "AI" also matches unrelated uses.
- History has only a handful of bubbles to compare with, so "unusual" rests on very few cases.
